newsitem.title: CUBA: Hurricane Lili pounds Cuba, heads towards Bahamas.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Lili pounds Cuba, heads towards Bahamas.

text.p: Hurricane Lili headed towards the central Bahamas on Friday afternoon after dumping heavy rains on Cuba and pounding parts of the island with wind gusts of up to 115 mph (185 kph), forecasters said.

The Miami-based National Hurricane Centre said that at 5 p.m. EDT (2100 GMT), the centre of Lili had just left Cuba's northern coast and was 125 miles (200 km) southwest of Andros Island in the Bahamas.
The hurricane was travelling east-northeast at 14 mph (22 kph) with sustained maximum winds of 90 mph (150 kph). Lili was likely to cross the central Bahamas within 12-24 hours.

"Some strengthening is possible in the next 24 hours," the hurricane centre said. A hurricane warning remained in effect for the central and northwest Bahamas as well as for mainland Cuba from Matanzas province eastward to Camaguey.
Lili dumped up to 12 inches (30 cm) of rain in its path, causing flooding along Cuba's north coast, forecasters said.

The storm, which killed at least 10 people when it lashed Central America this week, did not appear to cause any casualties in Cuba. However, at least 20 houses collapsed in the city of Matanzas, 60 miles (100 km) east of Havana, the state news agency AIN said.

To the relief of Havana's two million inhabitants, the hurricane set a more easterly course than anticipated after hitting the Isle of Youth to the south late on Thursday. The provinces most affected so far by Lili were Matanzas, Cienfuegos, Sancti Spiritus and Villa Clara.

President Fidel Castro set off early on Friday to visit a town on the south coast threatened by the hurricane. He went on to the city of Matanzas and then Varadero, where he met some of the 7,000 foreign tourists braving the storm.
Authorities on the Isle of Youth said they were assessing damage. A railway line was cut because of fallen trees and there were reports of damage to crops such as bananas.
On the Cuban mainland, sugar cane may also be affected by the hurricane. The cane, a crucial hard currency earner for Cuba, is within two or three months of being harvested.

Havana was a wind-blown ghost town early on Friday. Some streets were littered with tree branches and several electricity poles fell during the night. The state electricity company cut power to most parts of the capital before dawn to minimise damage to power lines during the storm's passage.
By mid-morning, some residents were venturing into the streets, but forecasters said Havana and other northern coastal areas should expect very high seas and possible flooding later in the day.
About 3,600 residents of the Malecon sea-front in Havana were evacuated from their homes and tourists at several sea-front hotels were relocated.

State radio said about 75,000 people had been evacuated from vulnerable buildings in Havana despite initial reluctance on the part of many people living in decaying buildings to leave their homes. Overall, about 176,000 people were evacuated from their homes in Cuba and Havana international airport was closed until further notice.
So far Lili caused the highest death toll in Nicaragua, where Civil Defence officials said five people had drowned in swollen rivers across the country.
In Costa Rica, four people were killed in river tragedies and in Honduras a toddler died when his house was washed away in a shantytown on the edge of the capital Tegucigalpa.
In the Bahamas, schools closed early, tourist flights were cancelled and customers crowded into food stores and gasoline stations.
